messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mariana was twenty-one years old, working as an animator at a small studio in Los Angeles, when she finally walked into a therapist’s office. She had spent most of her life trying not to think about what she had seen as a child. She was seven when her mother’s boyfriend, a man named Carlos, had thrown a glass bottle against the kitchen wall during an argument. Mariana had been hiding behind the sofa, and she remembered the sharp smell of alcohol and citrus as the bottle shattered, the way the shards glittered on the linoleum. She had not seen Carlos since that night, but the memory had never left her. It did not feel like a memory, really—it felt more real than ordinary things, more immediate, as if she could still smell that citrus-and-alcohol tang when she let her mind drift too close. She had learned to push it away before she could fully recall it, blocking the image mid-frame, but the effort left her exhausted. Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away. After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me.

Over the years, Mariana had developed a quiet set of rules to keep herself steady. She avoided making any plans for the future—no vacations, no weekend trips, no dinner reservations more than a day ahead—because every time she tried, she felt a tightness in her chest that told her something bad would happen. She also controlled her eating strictly, counting calories and skipping meals when she felt anxious, because it was the one thing she could manage. And she avoided anything that reminded her of Carlos: certain colognes, the sound of glass clinking, even the color of the shirt he had worn that night. At work, a colleague once tossed a crumpled ball of paper across the room, and Mariana flinched so hard she knocked over her coffee. The sudden movement had made her heart pound as if she were seven years old again, hiding behind the sofa. She became hypervigilant after that, scanning the open-plan office for any unexpected motion, and her irritability spiked—she snapped at a coworker who tapped her shoulder to get her attention, and she felt a hot, angry shame afterward that she could not shake.

The triggers came in waves. A photo of a broken vase on Instagram. The sound of a bottle being uncorked at a restaurant. The smell of citrus in a cleaning product at a friend's house sent the whole night flooding back before she had even registered what she was smelling. Each cue sent her heart into her throat, her body reading it as an emergency even when her mind knew there was nothing to fear. Each time, the memory surged back with that vivid, olfactory clarity—the smell of citrus and alcohol—and Mariana felt helpless all over again. She had come to believe that she could not deal with even the slightest upset, that any disruption would unravel her completely. The avoidance had kept her safe, in her nervous system's accounting, which meant the danger they were responding to must be real and ongoing. Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it. And the worst part was the certainty that the people responsible—Carlos, her mother for letting him into the house—had faced no consequences. That injustice sat inside her like a stone. When the memory came, she would restrict her eating even more, as if controlling her body could control the past, and she would cancel any tentative plans she had made, retreating into her apartment where nothing could surprise her. But the hypervigilance followed her there too. She slept with her back to the wall, and any unexpected sound—a car backfiring, a neighbor dropping something—made her startle, which triggered the memory again, which made her feel even more helpless.

The cycle tightened over months. Mariana found herself avoiding more and more: she stopped going to the grocery store at certain hours, stopped answering calls from friends, stopped opening her mailbox because a flyer for a home-decor store showed a picture of a glass vase. At work, she began to eat lunch at her desk, alone, because the communal kitchen had a cabinet full of glass cups that someone might drop. On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome. She was sure that if she let her guard down, something terrible would happen—she could not stop bad things from happening to her, and the only safety was in control. When the threat felt this close, scanning the room for escape routes wasn't a symptom — it was just sensible. The irritability made her difficult to work with, and her supervisor had pulled her aside to ask if everything was all right. Mariana had said yes, but she knew it was not true. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at her desk, staring at a storyboard she had been too afraid to finish because it involved a character throwing a plate. She had sat there for an hour, frozen, the smell of citrus and alcohol filling her nose, and she realized she could not keep living this way. She was most afraid that therapy would not work—that she would always be this vigilant, this hungry, this alone. But she was also afraid of what might happen if she did not try.
